before: Pandita Ramabai was an Indian scholar and reformer, born into a high-caste Hindu family, who became a Christian and gave her life to women and children in need. She founded the Mukti Mission near Pune. It cared for widows, orphans and girls rescued from hardship. She was a Bible translator and a woman of deep prayer.

Minnie Abrams was an American missionary who worked with Ramabai. In 1905 prayer circles at Mukti sought a fuller outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and a revival followed. Those who were there reported repentance, intense prayer and spiritual gifts, including speaking in tongues. Abrams wrote about it in *The Baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire* (1906). Her book teaches that the Spirit's coming gives power for witness and holy living, and it spread the news to other countries. Later Abrams went to Chile, where her writings and letters reached the Methodists in Valparaiso whom we meet in Unit 6. This is one reason historians speak of Mukti as part of a worldwide network, not a separate local event.

before: After Mukti, the Pentecostal message grew in many parts of India, and the south, especially the state of Kerala, became a major center. Kerala already had old Christian communities, and many of their members were drawn to the Pentecostal message. Indian leaders formed their own churches. One of the best known is the Indian Pentecostal Church of God, founded in 1924 under K. E. Abraham. Other Indian Pentecostal groups and many independent churches followed. Some had links with missionaries from the West, and many did not.

The name was adopted in 1934 and the organization was registered in 1935. Other Indian Pentecostal groups and many independent churches followed. Some had links with missionaries from the West, and many did not. [U8.2]

before: Protestant Christianity reached Korea in the late 1800s. In 1907 a great revival came to Pyongyang among Presbyterians and Methodists. Congregations gathered for long prayer, and many believers publicly confessed their sins with tears. This revival was not Pentecostal in the strict sense, because it did not teach the doctrine of Spirit baptism with tongues as we do. But it left Korean Christians with a habit of fervent, early-morning and persistent prayer. This habit still marks the Korean church today, Pentecostal and non-Pentecostal.

before: The best known Korean Pentecostal is David Yonggi Cho (also called Paul Yonggi Cho). In 1958 he began a church in Seoul with Choi Ja-sil, who became his co-worker and mother-in-law. It began in a poor part of the city, in a tent. The church later moved to Yoido Island in Seoul and grew into the Yoido Full Gospel Church, which for years was reported to be one of the largest congregations in the world. These figures were given by the church itself, so we should treat them as estimates and not as audited counts.

before: Cho's life also teaches a warning. In his later years Korean courts examined the church's finances, and in 2014 a court found him guilty in a case involving church money. We do not need to say more here. We need to say that honest historians must record both the fruit and the failures, and that a famous leader is still a man who must be held accountable. We will return to this in Unit 10 when we study teaching about prosperity.
after: Cho’s later life also raises questions of accountability. In February 2014 a Seoul court sentenced him to three years in prison, suspended for five years, after finding him guilty in a case involving church officials’ purchase of shares owned by his eldest son at about four times their market value. Contemporary reports describe the case as embezzlement or breach of trust; this course reports the transaction and sentence without adding legal conclusions beyond those sources. This finding is included as an example of accountability, not as an explanation of Cho’s theology. Scholars and Pentecostals have debated whether his “threefold blessing” should be classified as prosperity teaching or understood as a contextual Korean Pentecostal theology. Unit 10 returns to that debate. [U8.5]

before: **The True Jesus Church.** It began in 1917 in Beijing and spread widely. It emphasizes speaking in tongues and healing. Its leaders were Chinese. It also holds teachings that classical Trinitarian Pentecostals cannot accept, including a Oneness view of God. We include it in the history because it was an early Chinese Pentecostal-type church, and we say plainly that it is not part of our family of faith on this point.

**The Jesus Family.** It was founded in the 1920s in Shandong province by a Chinese leader named Jing Dianying. Its members lived together in communities, shared their goods, worked on farms, and practiced prayer and healing. It was ended as an organization under the new government in the early 1950s.
after: **The True Jesus Church.** It began in Beijing in 1917 and emphasizes speaking in tongues and healing. Its leaders were Chinese. It also holds a Oneness view of God, which classical Trinitarian Pentecostals reject. We include it as an early Chinese Pentecostal-type movement and state our theological disagreement plainly. [U8.6]

**The Jesus Family.** Jing Dianying began a predecessor Christian association in Shandong in 1921; the communal movement known as the Jesus Family developed in the 1920s. Members formed communal households, shared property, worked together, and practiced prayer and healing. Its organized communal life was brought to an end by the early 1950s. [U8.7]

before: **Indonesia.** Pentecostal churches began early in the twentieth century and grew over many decades. A widely known revival came to the island of Timor in 1965, during a time of national crisis, with reports of repentance, healing and powerful preaching. Today Pentecostal and charismatic churches are a large part of Indonesian Protestantism.

**The Philippines.** The Philippines is mainly a Roman Catholic nation. Pentecostal missions began in the early twentieth century, and today there are both Pentecostal churches and a very large Catholic charismatic movement. We study the charismatic stream further in Unit 9.
**Singapore, Malaysia and other places.** Many Pentecostal and charismatic churches grew in the cities in the later twentieth century.
after: **Indonesia.** Pentecostal churches began in the early twentieth century and grew over many decades. A major revival associated with Timor in 1965 is documented in a historical study that also describes the event as controversial and weighs spiritual, social, and political explanations. Reports include repentance, healing, and powerful preaching; no single-cause explanation or exact size is asserted here. [U8.8]

**The Philippines.** The Philippines is mainly Roman Catholic. Pentecostal missions are documented from 1921, with an Assemblies of God missionary arriving in 1926. Today the country includes Pentecostal churches and a large Catholic charismatic movement. We study the charismatic stream further in Unit 9. [U8.9]
**Other Southeast Asian settings.** Pentecostal and charismatic history varies by country. This unit does not attempt a national chronology for every Southeast Asian community.

before: Asian Pentecostalism has many roots and many leaders. At Mukti in 1905, Pandita Ramabai and Minnie Abrams saw a revival of prayer and spiritual gifts, joined with mercy to widows and orphans. Indian Pentecostal churches, such as the Indian Pentecostal Church of God founded in 1924 under K. E. Abraham, grew through Indian leadership, especially in Kerala. In Korea, the 1907 Pyongyang revival prepared a praying church; after the Korean War, David Yonggi Cho and Choi Ja-sil began the church that became Yoido Full Gospel Church, known for cell groups and prayer, though its famous leader later faced a court case about church finances. In China, the True Jesus Church, the Jesus Family and the house churches show Spirit-centered faith under pressure, but numbers are uncertain and the True Jesus Church teaches a Oneness view we cannot accept. In Southeast Asia, Indonesia, the Philippines and other nations show the same pattern of local ownership. We answer the claim that Asian Pentecostalism is a Western import by pointing to Asian origins and leaders, and we answer the worry about local religion by the test of Scripture.
after: Asian Pentecostalism has many roots and many leaders. At Mukti in 1905, Pandita Ramabai and Minnie Abrams saw a revival of prayer and spiritual gifts, joined with mercy to widows and orphans. Indian Pentecostal churches, including the fellowship that became the Indian Pentecostal Church of God, grew through Indian leadership, especially in Kerala; the church name and registration date to 1934–1935. In Korea, the 1907 Pyongyang revival prepared a praying church; after the Korean War, David Yonggi Cho and Choi Ja-sil began the church that became Yoido Full Gospel Church, known for cell groups and prayer, though its famous leader later faced a court case about church finances. In China, the True Jesus Church, the Jesus Family and the house churches show Spirit-centered faith under pressure, but numbers are uncertain and the True Jesus Church teaches a Oneness view we cannot accept. In Southeast Asia, the Indonesian and Philippine examples show how local believers shaped the movement after its arrival. We answer the claim that Asian Pentecostalism is a Western import by pointing to Asian origins and leaders, and we answer the worry about local religion by the test of Scripture.
